articles.title: James Gunn Shuts Down Rumors That Skydance Is Meddling With Man of Tomorrow
articles.summary: James Gunn has shut down rumors that the new DC overseers at Skydance have meddled with his cut of Man of Tomorrow following his shocking DC Studios exit.
articles.body:
James Gunn has shut down rumors that the new DC overseers at Skydance have meddled with his cut of Man of Tomorrow following his shocking DC Studios exit .

The internet has filled with gossip in the wake of Gunn and Peter Safran's departure as co-chairmen of the comic book entertainment wing earlier this week. As an ocean of rumors rises, some of the more worrying claims have seen some suggest Skydance has already taken control of the Superman director's sequel, which could result in major characters like Supergirl and Blue Beetle being cut entirely.

These are just some of the accusations that Gunn sought to dispel in a Threads post tonight. In what is essentially his first public statement since leaving DC Studios, the filmmaker took aim at the gossip that has DCU fans concerned. Not only have "sweeping changes" to Man of Tomorrow not been made, but apparently, no one at Skydance has even seen his movie yet.

"There are a lot of untrue rumors going around, but one of them is that Skydance has seen Man of Tomorrow and that all sorts of sweeping changes are being made," he said. "No one from Skydance has even seen the movie - the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. So any stories around this narrative are false."

It's a response that will not answer every question comic book movie enjoyers have about the future of the DCU, but it does clear the air about much of the more damning chatter online. Gunn's comments mean that any talk of Skydance being unhappy with the current cut of Man of Tomorrow is false. It also sounds like, at least for now, Supergirl and Blue Beetle, who had been previously reported to return, are safe.

With so much time left before David Corenswet's Clark Kent returns to theaters in July, though, it's hard to say how the Skydance takeover may impact its release. It's best to wait until Gunn or Skydance has more to share before setting any firm expectations in place for now.

All of that said, it's not too hard to see why fans of the DCU have felt uneasy in the last few days. Gunn and Safran have orchestrated the DCU to tell a varied collection of superpowered stories for four years, with its overarching plan for the years ahead only just starting to come into view. Pulling them from the driver's seat means the future is more unknown than ever before, especially considering Skydance was quick to find a replacement in Marvel alum Jeremy Latcham.

Will Man of Tomorrow be altered against Gunn's will? Will Skydance reboot the DC movie universe and scrap future plans for the DCU? How will any of this affect future entries in Robert Pattinson's The Batman saga? It's all too soon to tell, but that won't stop the rumor mill from pushing ahead.

What we do know is what Gunn shared with fans in the immediate aftermath of his exit. In a letter posted to social media , he promised that the characters he and Safran helped set up "will live on." He also confirmed that the duo was recently "engaged on another DC project" that he is writing. What that project is remains a mystery.

For more on the future of the DCU, you can read up on what we know about Latcham . You can also check out another report that suggested Skydance intends to prioritize more well-known heroes in the DC portfolio going forward . Man of Tomorrow, meanwhile, is set to premiere July 9, 2027.

Photo by Michael Kovac/Getty Images for Warner Bros. Pictures.

A Puppet's Wooden Heart is an optional side quest in the Phantom Blade 0 's Village of Lu. This quest can actually be easily missed as it requires you to trigger a conversation and then return to the character after you rest at a bell.

The character in question is the Songstress Puppet at the Temple of Blue Fireflies. Once you trigger her initial line of dialogue, rest at a bell and then talk to her again. She will give you a letter for Pei, beginning this quest.

Progress all the way through the outside of the Village of Lu until you free the third body and open the well. After exiting the building, take the zipline and jump down.

After delivering the letter, return to the Songstress Puppet at the Temple of Blue Fireflies and you will find a puppet talking to her. This appears to be Pei, whose body is now lost.

Travel back to the Engine Giant Remains bell and progress backwards. By the fire in the marshy area, you can find Pei's body with the Songstress Puppet's Letter book.

Return to the Songstress Puppet once again at the Temple of Blue Fireflies.

articles.title: Breaking Down Theo's Shock Moment in The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 and the Mystery of His Father With Actor Tyroe Muhafidin
articles.summary: A spoiler-filled The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 interview with Theo actor Tyroe Muhafidin.
articles.body:
Warning! Spoilers for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 Episodes 1-4 follow.

If you’re caught up with The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power , you’ll have watched Season 3, Episode 4 and were probably left reeling by a shock character death that leaves the elves in a spot of bother going into the final stretch.

During the first four episodes of Season 3, we see Theo, played by Tyroe Muhafidin, tempted by Sauron into becoming a Nazgnagôl. Nazgnagôl are men who wear one of Sauron’s Rings of Power, but still retain something of their humanity. That is, they are not fully Nazgûl, or Ringwraiths, as we know of the beings in the Third Age of J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-earth. They are, at this stage, Ring Servants.

Theo, last seen as a hopeful child of the Southlands and friend of hero elf Arondir, is now older and full of hate after five years of Númenórean oppression. Sauron sees something in him, something special, and offers Theo a gift. In Episode 2, appropriately called The Gift of Men, Sauron performs a dark ritual that lets Theo “meet” his mysterious father, or at least that’s what we think is happening here (with Sauron, you never really know!).

This is a callback to a scene in Season 1 where a young Theo encounters The Hilt, a broken sword-hilt forged during the First Age. It had been left hidden in a barn where Theo discovers it, and we see Theo’s blood drip into the Hilt, somehow feeding its regeneration. Clearly, Theo had some dark power inside him, although it was left unaddressed, sparking many fan theories over recent years.

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 Photos

In Season 3, Sauron notices the dark mark left on Theo’s arm after his interaction with The Hilt and immediately raises an eyebrow. Who was Theo’s father, really? During the ritual, Sauron uses the power of necromancy to communicate with the dead in the Unseen World. Sauron listens to the words of the dead, and tells Theo his father was named Fäldred, Son of Hammethreg. Theo asks, “Who are you, father?” The response, in Black Speech, is “Gorthmundur.” Sauron tells Theo this was a “Noble House of old, the sworn stewards of Mordor blessed with… certain powers.”

These powers, it seems, were passed down to Theo. “There is a reason you were drawn to that hilt, and it to you,” Sauron continues, before suggesting that Theo might have become ruler of the Southlands had his mother not “hidden the truth.” Theo responds to say his mother told him his father left. Sauron disputes this, before issuing a revelation that sends Theo spiralling: his mother murdered his father over what he had become.

Sauron, ever the opportunist, offers Theo a Ring of Power. He tells him that he has the power within him to become “a conqueror, a sorcerer, a king.” The downcast Theo accepts the gift.

Fast forward to Episode 4, and one of two shock deaths that punctuate this first block of The Rings of Power Season 3. Theo, now in full Nazgnagôl gear and spurred on by Sauron, murders his friend Arondir during the escape from Gundabad. It’s a shocking twist that cements Theo’s descent into darkness, and marks the end of the road for one of the mighty heroes of The Rings of Power.

In the interview below, I ask Tyroe Muhafidin about Theo’s journey in these first four episodes, what it’s like to play a Nazgnagôl, and where the murder of Arondir leaves The Rings of Power. And yes, we get into the question of Theo’s parentage. Was Sauron telling him the truth about his father?

IGN: The first question is an obvious one: how does it feel to be playing a Nazgnagôl?

Tyroe Muhafidin: It was crazy. The costume automatically gives you a sense of such great strength and power. The biggest thing for me was, as soon as I put on those gauntlets there was an automatic transforming moment for me where you could just feel the power through your body. And it's interesting because I went from playing basically a helpless child to some godlike being. So it was a real jump and I had to do a lot of work in terms of my physicality and trying to look powerful and strong, which was something so new to me because I've always been scrawny and helpless. So yeah, it was a challenge, but I think I got there in the end, and I'm super, super grateful that I've got a chance to be something so iconic and to play something so iconic.

IGN: What is your understanding of what Nazgnagôl are, as it was explained to you?

Tyroe Muhafidin: So a Nazgûl directly translates to Ringwraith, whereas Nazgnagôl directly translates to Ring Servant. At this point in time when we've just put the ring on, we're not quite wraiths yet. We are still human men with autonomy over their body and can make their own decisions. We're just a lot stronger now. We've got a lot of power and a lot of dark power.

An important thing to know is at the beginning of this season, the One Ring hasn't yet been made. So these rings are yet to be binded completely to Sauron's will, where we are not now complete, I guess, his minions. We still have autonomy over who we are. That was the fun thing to play in this season, the gradual descent into more and more madness and more and more evil and darkness. But at this point in time, we get to very much still be people, just very strong people, I guess.

IGN: There's a really interesting scene where Sauron reveals Theo's parentage to him. What's your understanding of who Theo's father is? Sauron is suggesting at that moment that Theo has an innate power as a result of his parentage, but it's left ambiguous. And Sauron looks emotional even as he's talking to Theo about this. I almost was thinking he almost looks at him as his own son in some ways. So what's your read on that? What can you tell us about what all that means?

Tyroe Muhafidin: It's revealed that his father was the head of a few dark sorcerers and he sided with the dark side a long time ago, alongside his peers and the other Southlanders who sided with Sauron. And so there's that kind of information that's brought out.

But I think the big thing for Theo is when Sauron says his mother killed him when she found out. And I think that moment for me, and I think for Theo as a whole, it kind of sends a spin in the works of, what is Sauron really doing here and what is he trying to accomplish? Is he just trying to say words to make Theo happy, trying to build this broken boy up? Because he can see something for sure. And I don't think Theo really realizes. But I think there was always a dark side to Theo and maybe it was inherited, but that relationship to the Hilt was always something that stuck with him.

And I think maybe when he got a taste of that darkness in the Hilt, maybe it was the first time he kind of felt the presence of his father, and maybe that's why it was so addictive, that feeling to him. So I think this season we find out a little bit more of where he comes from.

But I think the biggest thing is, how much of it is the truth? What is Sauron saying that is manipulation and deceit and what is the truth? Which I think is kind of the fun dynamic of those scenes, is you feel like you're finding out a lot, but are you really?

IGN: There is a big moment in Episode 4 where Theo kills Arondir, a character who's been in the series from the beginning. When you first found out you'd be doing that, what was your reaction?

Tyroe Muhafidin: It was interesting. I was excited because I was like, "Oh, this is some juicy stuff to get into." But I think the moment I got the script, I found out and I was really excited because it was going to be some really cool stuff. When I read it all, it all became very real for me. And it was like, "Wow, this is a big task. This is super daunting." And there were months of intense anxiety coming up to this moment. But yeah, I guess I was just super excited, but anxious at the same time. And I feel like I knew at some point something big like this was going to happen. So I think it was just a matter of being prepared for it and trying to service Ismail [Cruz Córdova, who plays Arondir] as well, the best I possibly could.

IGN: What do you think the character death means for the show at that point and the story it's telling, but also for Theo? Do you see it as this is a moment that we see a tipping point in him that the audience is like, "Okay, yes, he has really gone too far."

Tyroe Muhafidin: In terms of the show, it's a moment of no-one is safe and there's no mercy from the dark side. And this war is very much real. The most talented and bravest of your warriors will go down. And that's kind of, I think, setting the premise for the rest of the war that's going to go on.

I think for Theo specifically, it definitely was that tipping point where his decision is made and his destiny is decided. And I think he realizes this afterwards as well, and whether he agrees with that decision he's made or not, he's made that decision.

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 episodes 1-4 are out now on Prime Video. Check back with IGN after Episodes 5 and 6 are released this week for more.

articles.title: ‘GTA VI’ Has Already Sold $1 Billion+ In Preorders—But May Not Revive Console Sales Amid AI-Driven Price Hikes
articles.summary: “Grand Theft Auto VI” may be the biggest video game launch of all time, but it comes as PlayStation and Xbox models are more expensive than ever thanks to an...
articles.body:
The highly anticipated release of "Grand Theft Auto VI" is sure to shatter records and thrill millions of gamers who have awaited the game's debut for over a decade—but it comes as game consoles are more expensive than ever, and analysts say it's unlikely even a blockbuster release like this will fix the gaming industry's AI-driven cost crisis.

After multiple delays, gamers will finally be able to play the long-awaited "Grand Theft Auto VI" on Nov. 19, ending a 13-year drought following the 2013 release of "Grand Theft Auto V."

The game will undoubtedly be the biggest release of the year, and possibly of all time—but it arrives at a moment of crisis for the gaming industry, as the rise of AI has caused a memory chip shortage that has sent console and game prices surging upward, creating a potential barrier to access for some players.

"Grand Theft Auto VI" sells in two price tiers—$80 for the standard edition, and $100 for the "ultimate" edition with additional in-game features—already making it the most expensive game in the series at launch.

That's not to mention the cost of the consoles compatible with the game: New PlayStation 5 and Xbox models cost between $599 and $899, much more expensive than they cost at launch, as both Sony and Microsoft have hiked prices amid the AI-fueled memory chip shortage and tariff pressures.

A gamer hoping to play "Grand Theft Auto VI" who hasn't yet bought one of the newer console models "has to fork out $500 to $900+ for a console plus $80 to $100 for the game," totaling "$580 to $1,000+ to get through the door, in a cost-of-living-squeezed market, at Christmas," Rhys Elliot, head of market analysis at gaming market intelligence firm Alinea Analytics, told Forbes.

As console sales have fallen amid price hikes, analysts told Forbes the anticipated release of "Grand Theft Auto VI" could offer a marginal boost, but it won't be enough for the industry to completely recover from cost pressures perpetrated by AI.

Why Are Game Consoles Getting So Expensive?

Largely because of AI. The surging demand for memory chips by AI data centers has siphoned supply from consumer products, meaning the prices of game consoles—as well as laptops, cell phones, and other electronic devices—have surged. The price increases have been particularly frustrating for gamers because conventional wisdom says game consoles will get cheaper over time, but the memory squeeze has bucked that trend. Since launch, all of the new-generation consoles, including the Xbox Series X and S, the PlayStation 5 and the Nintendo Switch 2, have become more expensive. The standard PlayStation 5 now costs $649.99, up from the $499.99 it cost at launch after Sony implemented two price hikes in under one year. The PlayStation 5 Pro cost $699.99 in 2024, but just two years later, it retails for a whopping $899.99. Microsoft also hiked Xbox prices twice in one year, saying in a June statement that "console storage and memory prices have increased by more than 2.5x and we expect another doubling by the fall of 2027." President Donald Trump's tariffs have also weighed on the cost of gaming consoles, which Sony's CFO Lin Tao said last year would impact the company's hardware, gaming and semiconductor production and may force price increases on consumer goods.

articles.title: This tiny gamepad with dual analog thumbsticks pushes the limits of portable controllers
articles.summary: CRKD makes modern dual-stick controllers extremely portable with its full-featured $30 Atom Plus, but expect some finger contortioning with larger hands.
articles.body: As much as I appreciate the ingenious design of the Nintendo Switch’s Joy-Con, my family and I can’t stand using them as standalone gamepads. So when we travel with the Switch 2, we always bring at least one full-size gamepad, plus a couple of 8BitDo’s Zero 2 controllers for games that don’t use analog thumbsticks. I’ve spent years hunting for an alternative that pairs the size of the Zero 2 with as much of the functionality of a larger controller as I can get, and CRKD’s new Atom Plus is nearly exactly that. But if you have larger hands like I do, you may find the gamepad’s focus on portability a struggle. [Product: CRKD Atom Plus | Measuring around 3.5 inches wide, the $29.99 Atom Plus is about a half-inch smaller than the 8BitDo Zero 2 but squeezes in considerably more features and functionality. The most obvious is a pair of symmetrical analog thumbsticks with anti-drift tunneling magnetoresistance technology. You also get shoulder buttons and triggers, rumble feedback, a dedicated home button, motion controls, and customization through a mobile app. [Image: The 8BitDo Zero 2 gamepad (bottom) is still much smaller than the Atom Plus (top) but lacks triggers and thumbsticks. Like many third-party controllers, the Atom Plus works with multiple platforms, including the Switch and Switch 2, PCs, Android, iOS, and various smart TVs. And just like other gamepads, pairing to different devices requires putting the Atom Plus into one of several Bluetooth modes by holding down a combination of buttons at power-up, which in this case is the home button plus a specific direction on the D-pad. It’s easy to do, but never easy to remember: I frequently needed to grab the manual or quickly Google which direction I need to press when switching devices. The Atom Plus already features a bunch of technical info etched into the back of the controller, so I’d love to see these important pairing instructions included there, too. (And that goes for all multiplatform gamepads.) [Image: The thumbsticks on the Atom Plus (center) are nearly identical in size to those on the original Switch’s Joy-Con (right) but smaller than the thumbsticks on the Switch 2 (left). I primarily tested the Atom Plus with the Nintendo Switch 2 since I mostly plan to use the controller as a travel accessory. The thumbsticks are about the same size as those on the original Switch Joy-Con, which means they’re smaller than the Switch 2’s. And while I prefer an asymmetrical layout, the Atom Plus’ sticks are very good, with a little more tension than Nintendo’s that I find actually helps with precision movements given their limited travel. [Image: At times, the Atom Plus’ layout can feel a little too crowded. I often found my thumb bumping other controls and buttons when playing with the D-pad. While the overall build quality feels excellent, the Atom Plus’ tiny footprint creates some compromises and challenges. The front action buttons and D-pad feel nice and squishy, but the gamepad’s controls are a little crowded. When pressing down or right on the D-pad, my thumb regularly bumps the left thumbstick. It doesn’t hinder gameplay, but I do find it an annoying distraction. [Image: The shoulder buttons and digital triggers sit at different heights, but I still found myself accidentally pressing both at times. The shoulder buttons use digital microswitches, as do the triggers, which means the latter can’t be used for racing games that support analog acceleration controls. I like that the two sets of buttons on the top edge sit at slightly different heights, but I would have preferred a little more differentiation since I’ve occasionally accidentally pressed the triggers when I meant to hit the shoulder buttons. [Image: Connecting the Atom Plus to CRKD’s mobile app lets you remap its controls, turn certain features on or off, and update its firmware. I was impressed with the Atom Plus’ customizability, however. When paired to an accompanying mobile app, you can check the controller’s remaining charge, turn off rumble feedback, see its unique product number (by tapping your phone to an NFC chip inside the controller), and remap any of its controls. That includes the pair of dual-function shortcut levers that replicate the Switch’s plus and minus buttons and screenshot shortcut. [Image: The Atom Plus (top) is excellent for travel but not nearly as comfortable as a full-size controller. Those levers move up and down and cleverly reduce the number of buttons crowding the front of the Atom Plus, but they feel a little too small, which is more or less the general theme. It’s a tiny gamepad that’s great for travel or stashing in your everyday carry. But, unsurprisingly, it probably won’t find its way into your regular gaming rotation. It’s assumed that players will be willing to settle for the compromise of occasionally contorting their fingers in weird, new ways for one of the smallest fully featured controllers on the market. [Image: If you aren’t sold on using the Nintendo Switch’s Joy-Con as standalone gamepads, the Atom Plus is an excellent travel accessory. I don’t think a dual-stick controller could get any smaller than the Atom Plus without making too many ergonomic compromises. So while I applaud CRKD for the careful balancing act behind the Atom Plus’ design, and would certainly recommend it for those wanting a very capable controller that’s also cheap and portable, I’m now curious how it compares to Microsoft’s recently announced Xbox Nano controller that’s “surprisingly comfortable,” according to The Verge’s Tom Warren. It’s $20 more expensive than CRKD’s and noticeably larger, but it adds analog triggers, a more spacious design, and stubby grips making it easier to hold for those of us with beefy mitts. Photos by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge

One optional fight in Phantom Blade Zero in Acolyte Yanru. This is a fight that forms a part of the Purple Story Quest Secrets At the Heart of the Lake . While optional, this fight holds a story item that unlocks a late game area, therefore it is highly suggested that you fight her.

Unlike most fights in the game this is not a sword-on-sword fight, instead with you dodging her various fire attacks.

Yanru is located between the Terraces and Engine Giant Remains bells.

Head south from the latter, and stick to the left to find a marsh with the scarecrow. Interact with it to be teleported to the fight.

Acolyte Yanru is not a complex fight, but she will deal fire damage which can be hard to manage and has a lot of screen-covering attacks as it flies around and launches fireballs at you. Realistically, though you should be able to defeat them with a weapon level at around level 8-12. Any weapon and any Phantom Edges work for this fight as you can easily overwhelm her. You just want to stick behind them or run and dodge around them at all times.

Here are the special moves that you need to know about for phase one.

But, after that attack she will launch a larger fireball at you which hits the ground and tracks you. It doesn't detonate until around a second after it lands, allowing you to dodge out from within its radius.

As mentioned, her moveset is quite simple. There are no opportunities to parry and this fight relies completely on dodging and making the most of her openings. In reality, Yanru is very easy to stun and you can often keep her stunned with complete heavy attack combos, perfomring three or four combos back-to-back. Pair that with some Phantom Edge moves and special attacks and you will soon be attacking more than her.

Keep to her back, keep dodging, and make the most of her Flaming Circle unblockable attacks to land those counter moves.

articles.summary: Crimson Desert's Charting the Unknown DLC reviewed by Travis Northup on PC and Xbox Series X, also available on PlayStation 5."Crimson Desert’s Charting the Unknown DLC is unlikely to win over anyone who hadn’t already fallen in love with this massive world, but it does successfully expand a game that already had a staggering amount of stuff to do. Diving around underwater ruins and exploring islands for treasure is a good time, even if the ship exploration and combat on the way to that seafaring content is a bore. Elsewhere, some of the new activities like a business management minigame and NPC dating are absolutely worth adding to your backlog of quests to tackle. Those side distractions continue to be the true appeal of Crimson Desert, but it’s a shame that the new story questlines that act as an extended epilogue are largely as dull as they are inaccessible. Overall, Charting the Unknown is just more Crimson Desert, with its “jack of all trades, master of none” philosophy fully intact. If you’re hundreds of hours deep and that’s all you want, it will almost certainly deliver – but if you’re not, it’s not the most convincing reason to come back."
